title: Hosting rubric + success metrics — Falcon Factory POC
summary: Initial POC scoping focused on workload sizing, benchmark plan and decision criteria between Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployment modes. Primary goals: define success metrics (latency/throughput/quality), agree benchmark harness, and align on timeline and security gating for a 6-week pilot.
action_items: Maya — send benchmark harness template and example scripts (due 2026-02-02)
Luis — draft recommended batching/quantization profiles for their 2k token tail requests (due 2026-02-05)
Priya — provide 1 week of anonymized request logs and a sample prompt set (due 2026-02-03)
Rajiv — confirm VPC peering and egress policy constraints and share network diagram (due 2026-02-06)
Daniel — confirm pilot success criteria and internal stakeholders for sign-off (due 2026-02-09)
next_steps: Share Redwood security pack (SOC2/ISO) and architecture brief
Run initial hosted baseline benchmarks next week using Redwood-provided harness
Schedule 2-hour technical workshop (SE-led) to walk through dedicated/private deployment checklist

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Alvarez (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (CTO, Falcon Factory), Priya Sinha (ML Engineer), Rajiv Menon (Infra Lead), Elena Gomez (Product PM)

Summary: Discussed POC scope focusing on hosting choice (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private), defined benchmarks, success metrics and timeline. Agreed to run hosted baseline then evaluate dedicated/private if needed for compliance/perf.

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick round of intros — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and Luis is our senior SE.
[00:18] Daniel: Hey all, Daniel here. We'll be talking about our inference stack and what a pilot looks like.
[00:25] Priya: Priya, ML infra and models. We've been running a couple of open models locally.
[00:31] Rajiv: Rajiv, infra. Mainly network and security questions from our side.
[00:36] Elena: Elena — product, looking at success metrics and timelines.

[02:15] Luis: Cool. To frame the convo: we usually recommend starting with a hosted baseline to get realistic p50/p95 numbers then move to dedicated if you need predictable throughput/cost or to private if you have strict VPC/on-prem rules. We want to size the workload and pin down success criteria.

[04:02] Priya: Short intro to our workload — it's a multi-turn assistant for operators, avg prompt ~350 tokens, tail up to 2k tokens for long diagnostics. Peak concurrent users around 30 internal users but we expect public beta to see 40–60 QPS on some flows. Latency-wise product wants sub-300ms for p50 on short prompts, but they're okay with 500–700ms on longer ones.

[05:12] Maya: That helps. Two immediate flags — short prompt SLOs are pretty tight and will influence kernel selection and batching choices. For hosted, we can often hit those for small context sizes; longer tails will push cost up.

[06:05] Rajiv: On security, we need VPC peering and customer-managed keys for production. SOC2 is a must. Also some records will need to stay in-region.

[07:00] Luis: Good to call out. Our private deployment supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem as an option for air-gapped. For the POC we can keep data in-region via hosted region selection, but private is the clear path if they require no egress.

[08:45] Elena: Can you give a rough cost delta between hosted and dedicated for our workload? We want ballpark to decide if it's worth pushing to dedicated.

[09:12] Maya: Roughly, for the profile you described, hosted might be 1.0x baseline per-token cost with some variance; dedicated can reduce unit cost by 20–40% at steady throughput but requires commit and capacity sizing. There's also ops overhead for private. Luis, add detail?

[09:44] Luis: Yes, dedicated helps when you have predictable utilization and long KV cache reuse. Also quantization helps — if we can accept an int8 profile for some flows, you might see another 10–20% improvement. But there's a risk of quality regression which Priya should validate.

[11:30] Priya: We can run quantization tests. Our quality bar is fairly strict: no more than 2% deviation on key metrics (intent detection, slot extraction) vs current baseline.

[12:10] Daniel: Benchmarks — what do you need from us to start the hosted baseline?

[12:27] Luis: Ideally: one week of anonymized request logs, a sample prompt set for short and long flows, and an expected concurrency profile. We provide a harness that can replay requests preserving timing. Maya will send the template.

[13:05] Maya: I'll share the harness and a starter script. We also have a spreadsheet template for capturing p50/p95/p99, throughput, token cost, and error rates.

[14:40] Rajiv: Network constraints — egress, firewall rules, and VPC peering. For hosted we need a plan for secure peering; for private we want the checklist.

[15:10] Luis: We'll produce a checklist for Dedicated and Private deployment: network ports, peering, KMS setup, audit log endpoints, and a sizing guide for GPU pools.

[16:55] Elena: Timeline? What's realistic for a POC to produce numbers we can sign off on?

[17:12] Maya: From experience: week 0 onboarding + infra setup, week 1 hosted baseline and quick perf tests, weeks 2–3 deeper benchmarks and quality/regression tests, week 4 analysis and decision. So about 4–6 weeks total. You mentioned you wanted to target mid-February — that aligns.

[18:30] Daniel: That timeline works. What's the success criteria we'd present to execs?

[18:45] Priya: I'll push for quality first — thresholds we discussed: <2% regression. Product wants latency p50 <300ms on 350 token prompts and p95 <700ms on longer flows. Ops wants deterministic throughput of 50 sustained QPS with graceful degradation above that.

[19:54] Luis: For benchmarks we'll capture: p50/p95/p99, token cost / 1k tokens, GPU utilization, KV-cache hit rates, and end-to-end error rates. We'll also run a stress test to see tail latencies at 2x expected load.

[21:30] Rajiv: For private deployment, our blockers are procurement for on-prem hardware and legal review. How long to stand up Private in parallel?

[21:50] Maya: Private typically needs more time — procurement + setup could be 8–12 weeks. Dedicated is the middle ground: reserved capacity on Redwood with VPC peering can be live in 2–4 weeks depending on approvals.

[23:05] Priya: Ok. So approach: start hosted baseline immediately, then evaluate dedicated if cost/latency tradeoffs justify it; reserve private only if compliance or data residency forces it.

[24:30] Elena: About fallbacks — if dedicated nodes hit capacity, does Redwood have model variant fallback or regional fallback?

[24:50] Luis: Yes — automatic fallback policies exist. We can route to a cheaper quantized variant or a different region. We'll document fallback SLOs and how that maps to correctness expectations.

[26:18] Maya: Also noting caching strategy: automatic prefix/KV caching can cut downstream token compute by up to 30% depending on reuse patterns. Priya, your logs will show reuse.

[27:35] Priya: We have about 25% prefix reuse in common operator flows, the long diagnostics are unique. So caching will help short prompts.

[29:00] Daniel: What about monitoring and observability during the pilot? We need per-route latency and token cost dashboards.

[29:20] Luis: Redwood Console provides per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost breakdown, traces and error analysis. We'll give you temporary access and a dashboard template.

[30:05] Maya: We'll also capture a small eval set of golden prompts for automated regression checks as part of the harness.

[31:40] Priya: Regarding bench harness — does it emulate multi-turn conversation with KV cache warm-up?

[31:52] Luis: Yes, the harness supports session-based replay and KV cache warming. We'll include a mode for cold-start vs warmed caches.

[33:05] Rajiv: Any network bandwidth expectations for sustained 50 QPS with 2k token tails? That's important for our infra planning.

[33:20] Luis: Rough estimate: worst-case egress ~ (tokens * avg size) — we'll provide a calculator. For 50 QPS with 2k average tokens you'll want to plan for significant bandwidth; for mixed workloads it's less. We'll send numbers.

[34:50] Elena: Risk register — what are the top risks for the pilot?

[35:06] Maya: I'd call out three: quality regression with quantization, unexpected tail latency at scale, and procurement delays for private options. We can mitigate with staged testing and fallback policies.

[36:40] Daniel: Any legal/compliance docs we should expect?

[36:52] Maya: We'll share SOC2 report, encryption and KMS details, data flow diagrams, and a PCA contract addendum if needed.

[38:10] Priya: For evaluation metrics, add intent detection F1 and slot accuracy; these are the ones that matter for product.

[38:40] Luis: Noted. We'll add those to the results spreadsheet as custom metrics.

[40:00] Elena: Ok let's recap decisions and next steps.

[40:10] Maya: Recap: 1) Falcon Factory will provide logs + prompt set; 2) Redwood will run hosted baseline week-of 2026-02-02; 3) SE-led workshop to discuss Dedicated/Private checklist scheduled for next week; 4) success criteria agreed: latency p50 <300ms short prompts, p95 <700ms long prompts, quality delta <2%, throughput 50 sustained QPS.

[41:05] Daniel: Sounds good. Any objections?

[41:12] Rajiv: No. Need to confirm network diagram by Friday.

[42:00] Priya: I'll assemble the prompt goldset and anonymize logs — aim to send by 2026-02-03.

[43:15] Luis: I'll put together the quantization/batching recommendations and the harness instructions (due 02-05).

[44:30] Maya: I'll send the security pack and the benchmark template after this call. Also will propose times for the technical workshop.

[45:50] Elena: One last question — if hosted baseline looks promising, how fast can we switch to dedicated?

[46:05] Maya: If you decide within the pilot window and sign a reserved commitment, we can move you to dedicated in as little as 2 weeks for small GPU pools. For larger reserved capacity it's 3–4 weeks.

[47:10] Daniel: Thanks everyone, this is helpful. We'll follow up on the action items.
[47:20] Maya: Thanks all. We'll share notes and next step calendar invites.

[47:45] (meeting ends)
